summary: Presents a mechanism for OSPF to hide transit-only networks, meaning networks that connect only routers. Such networks are usually given routable addresses that appear in LSAs but are not needed for data traffic, and they can be targeted by remote attacks, so hiding them reduces the exposure.

eli5.summary: The hallways only staff use do not need to be on the public map. Keeping them off the map means strangers cannot find and bother them.

questions: how to hide transit networks in ospf
what is a transit-only network in ospf
what is the 255.255.255.255 mask in an ospf network-lsa
does hiding a prefix in ospf affect reachability
subtitle: How OSPF routers stop advertising the router-to-router links that only they need, so the prefixes never reach routing tables.

tldr.problem: In OSPF, networks that connect only routers (transit-only networks) usually carry routable IP addresses that are advertised in LSAs but are not needed for data traffic. Remote attackers can send packets to those addresses.
tldr.mechanism: For point-to-point and point-to-multipoint links, the router leaves the stub (Type 3) link out of its router-LSA. For broadcast and NBMA networks, the Designated Router puts the special mask 255.255.255.255 in the network-LSA, and receivers do not install that route. In OSPFv3 the IPv6 prefixes are left out of the LSAs.
tldr.outcome: The prefixes are not installed in the routing tables on OSPF routers, which speeds up convergence and reduces exposure to remote attacks, without affecting reachability to end hosts. In OSPFv2 some IPv4 addresses can still be visible.

today: RFC 6860 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2013. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it updates RFC 2328 and RFC 5340.

sections.title: Why Hide Transit-Only Networks
sections.content:
A transit-only network is a network that connects routers only. In OSPF these networks are usually given routable IP addresses. Those addresses are advertised in Link State Advertisements (LSAs), but data traffic does not need them. They also give attackers a target: remote attacks can be launched against routers by sending packets to these networks.

RFC 6860 describes a mechanism to hide them, to speed up network convergence and reduce vulnerability to remote attacks. Hiding does not impact reachability to end hosts.

In this document, 'hiding' means the prefixes are not installed in the routing tables on OSPF routers. In OSPFv2 the IPv4 interface addresses are still visible in the Router-LSA links and in the network-LSA Link-State ID. In OSPFv3 the router-LSAs and network-LSAs do not contain IPv6 addresses, so nothing is visible there. The RFC updates RFC 2328 (OSPFv2) and RFC 5340 (OSPFv3).
sections.eli5: Some roads are only used by the routers themselves. Putting them on every map just shows troublemakers where to knock, so this RFC says to leave them off.

sections.title: Point-to-Point Networks in OSPFv2
sections.content:
A point-to-point network joins a single pair of routers. For each numbered point-to-point network, a router normally puts two link descriptions in its router-LSA: a Type 1 link (point-to-point) describing the neighbor router, and a Type 3 link (stub) describing the assigned IPv4 subnet. The Type 1 link is used for the SPF calculation, while the Type 3 link is used to install a route to the subnet in the Routing Information Base (RIB).

To hide a transit-only point-to-point network, the router simply omits the Type 3 link from its router-LSA. The neighbor link stays, so the topology still works, but no route to the subnet is installed.
sections.eli5: Two friends share a private tunnel. The map still says they are connected, but it no longer lists the tunnel's street address.

sections.title: Broadcast and NBMA Networks: the Special Mask
sections.content:
A broadcast network joins more than two routers and can address one physical message to all of them. A Designated Router (DR) describes it in a network-LSA. OSPF gets the network number from the combination of the Link State ID and the network mask, and the Link State ID is also used for the two-way connectivity check.

To hide a transit-only broadcast network, the special subnet mask 255.255.255.255 MUST be used in the network-LSA. Because the Link State ID does not change, the two-way connectivity check proceeds normally. Using that mask also means an access broadcast network (one with hosts on it) is not hidden by accident.

On receipt, a router MUST calculate the routing table normally, but if the network mask is 255.255.255.255 it MUST NOT install the route in the RIB. The RFC recommends that all routers in an area be upgraded at the same time. NBMA networks, where OSPF emulates a broadcast network with a Designated Router, use the same modification.
sections.eli5: The group's meeting room is marked on the map with a code that says 'do not drive here'. Everyone still knows who is in the group, but no road leads to the room.

sections.title: Point-to-Multipoint Networks and Partial Deployment
sections.content:
In point-to-multipoint mode, OSPF treats a non-broadcast network as a collection of point-to-point links. A router has one Type 1 link for each directly communicable router, plus one Type 3 stub link advertising its own interface address with the mask 255.255.255.255. To hide the network, the Type 3 link is omitted from the router-LSA.

The RFC also considers routers that have not been upgraded. If one receives a modified network-LSA, it installs a host route to the originating DR. That is not ideal, but it is better than the previous result, which exposed the whole subnet. In a partial deployment the upgraded and non-upgraded routers disagree, which creates routing black holes. Here the RFC argues they actually help, because packets for the transit-only networks are dropped somewhere in the network, which helps the DRs defend themselves from remote attacks. It concludes the change is backward compatible with OSPFv2.
sections.eli5: If a few people have not got the new map yet, they might still find one door, but not the whole building. That is still better than before.

sections.title: Hiding Networks in OSPFv3
sections.content:
OSPFv3 removed addressing from the main packets and LSA types. Router-LSAs and network-LSAs only express topology. Addresses live in two other LSA types: the link-LSA, which associates IPv6 addresses with a link and has local-link flooding scope, and the intra-area-prefix-LSA, which associates IPv6 addresses with a router (by referencing a router-LSA) or with a broadcast or NBMA network (by referencing a network-LSA).

To hide a transit-only network in OSPFv3, the IPv6 prefixes are omitted from the router-LSA. As a result the Designated Router leaves them out when it builds an intra-area-prefix-LSA that references a network-LSA. A router building an intra-area-prefix-LSA that references a router-LSA MUST also omit the prefixes of the transit-only network.

The same mechanism works for OSPFv3 address families (RFC 5838), because each address family maps to a separate Instance ID and the existing LSAs are still used, so no new LSAs are needed.
sections.eli5: In the newer system the street names are on separate notes. To hide a hallway you just do not write its note.

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content:
Hiding networks reduces the ability to manage those interfaces. The RFC recommends also implementing extensions such as RFC 5837, which can give a user the address of an interface. Even if such an address is hidden, it is assigned to the interface but will not be reachable.

  • Forwarding address: an AS-external-LSA or NSSA-LSA can carry a non-zero forwarding address, and a matching routing table entry must exist for the SPF calculation. When prefix hiding is configured on the next-hop interface, the next-hop address MUST NOT be advertised as a forwarding address, so routing to some external routes may be sub-optimal.
  • Virtual links: a virtual link needs matching routing table entries for its endpoints. If prefix hiding is configured on an interface, the endpoint MUST NOT use that interface's IP address as the virtual interface address.
  • Unnumbered interfaces: no host route is generated for them and no IP packets can be addressed to them, so they are already hidden. A numbered interface they point to (for example a loopback) can be hidden by these mechanisms or by not advertising it, but its other uses, such as a virtual link endpoint or an inter-domain peering point, must be considered first.
sections.eli5: If a hallway is off the map, even the staff cannot easily walk to it for repairs. So check who else needs it before you hide it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Reducing vulnerability to remote attacks is one of the reasons for the document. Reachability information for transit-only networks is not installed in routers' forwarding tables, so even if an attacker knows the address of a transit-only network, the routers have no forwarding information to reach it. In some cases the address is omitted from the LSA entirely.

Some information cannot be omitted, such as the OSPF Router ID. It may be taken from an IPv4 address on the router, but the configuration can easily be changed. The steps could also be used to hide networks that are not transit-only, so the RFC expects users to take the same care as with other routing protocol parameters.
sections.eli5: A stranger who knows a secret hallway's name still cannot get there if no road leads to it.
